messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi, a 53-year-old South Asian man, was a painter living in a small town with his wife. He had experienced significant trauma during his time as a civilian in a war zone, an event that had fundamentally altered the way he perceived the world around him. Ravi's traumatic experience involved being caught in the crossfire of gunfire and explosions, which left him feeling helpless and overwhelmed. Ravi’s life since then has been marked by intense triggers and maladaptive coping strategies. The smell of burning rubber or diesel fuel, reminiscent of the war zone, would often bring back vivid memories and plunge him into a state of hypervigilance. Each time he smelled these scents, his body would tense up, ready to react to perceived danger. This response was not just physical; it also triggered intense grief and an overwhelming sense that the world is dangerous. Ravi’s inability to control the situation during the traumatic event had led him to believe that he no longer possessed the capabilities that once defined him as a painter. He felt as though nothing in his life held any meaning anymore, leading him into a cycle of rumination about why this happened to him and an intense need to keep himself busy with other tasks to distract from these thoughts. His hyperalertness extended beyond olfactory triggers; loud bangs or sudden noises would cause him to startle violently. These sounds often brought back the memory of explosions, which made his body reenact the position he was in during those frightening moments. Each time this happened, Ravi felt a profound grief and an unsettling disbelief that such extreme events had actually occurred to him. The sense of loss of control and meaninglessness deeply affected Ravi’s daily life. He found himself avoiding news reports about conflicts or war because they reignited the feelings of vulnerability he experienced during the traumatic event. This avoidance, however, only deepened his negative appraisals that the world is dangerous and that he was no longer capable of doing what once defined him as a painter. Ravi’s coping mechanisms became self-reinforcing: the more he ruminated about why this happened to him, the harder it was for him to engage with his painting. His busyness and avoidance of news reports led him further away from his passion and into a deeper cycle of grief and hypervigilance. He would often find himself working late at night or on weekends, trying to keep his mind occupied and distracted from the memories that haunted him. This self-imposed isolation from his art began to affect his relationships with clients who had come to appreciate Ravi’s unique style and craftsmanship. His wife noticed changes in their daily interactions as well; he was more withdrawn and often preoccupied with thoughts of past events. What finally brought Ravi to seek help was a particularly distressing incident at work where the sound of a hammer hitting nails made him jump violently, causing him to drop his tools and feel an intense wave of grief. He realized that his hypervigilance and avoidance were interfering not just with his personal life but also his professional identity as a painter. Ravi was most afraid of losing control entirely and never being able to find meaning in his work or life again. However, he was hopeful that therapy could help him regain some sense of normalcy and allow him to reconnect with the world around him without feeling constantly on edge. He knew he needed support to break free from the cycles of rumination, avoidance, and hypervigilance that had taken over his life since his traumatic experience.
